objects.name: Subject Dies
objects.description:
Summary: The subject has died in connection with or as a result of activity.

Detail: This impact records the death of the subject where an analyst assesses a connection to the activity.

The most significant case is death which no person directly caused (e.g. through physical attack). Health and vaccine disinformation can lead people to act on a false treatment claim, or to decline an immunisation on the strength of a fabricated risk. Deaths of this kind can occur at considerable scale and be attributable to an information environment rather than to any single act identifiable against an individual.

Death can also follow from conditions the activity produced. A subject who dies of untreated illness in detention, or who dies after losing access to medical care when their finances were cut off, died as a consequence of the activity without being directly killed.

The impact also covers deaths where attribution is not yet possible. Early reporting frequently establishes that a subject died in connection with activity before it establishes how, and recording the death should not require a premature claim about its cause. Where later evidence establishes the route, the assessment should be revised to the more specific impact.

Example

After COVID-19 reached Iran in early 2020, a rumour circulated that drinking alcohol prevented or cured infection. Iran's national coroner's authority recorded [728 deaths from alcohol poisoning between 20 February and 7 April 2020, against 66 in the equivalent period the previous year.](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2020/04/iran-700-dead-drinking-alcohol-cure-coronavirus-200427163529629.html) A later academic study put the fuller toll at [more than 6,150 poisonings and 804 deaths by 20 May 2020, with methanol ingested in the belief it protected against the virus, and some survivors left blind.](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC8111183/) In some regions, [alcohol poisoning mortality exceeded COVID-19 mortality over the same period.](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC8111183/)

A second pattern, in which disinformation suppresses immunisation and an outbreak follows, is documented in Samoa. UNICEF reported [that measles vaccination coverage in Samoa fell to 40 per cent for the first dose and 28 per cent for the second dose in 2018,](https://reliefweb.int/report/samoa/pacific-measles-outbreak-unicef-supporting-government-samoa-respond-outbreak) after the country's immunisation programme was suspended following the deaths of two infants shortly after vaccination in July that year. The World Health Organization said [the resulting crisis was driven in part by an anti-vaccine group's messaging on social media, which used the infants' deaths to discourage vaccination.](https://news.un.org/en/story/2019/12/1052801) Samoa's Ministry of Health reported a [cumulative total of 5,707 confirmed measles cases and 83 deaths by 20 January 2020, in a population of about 200,000.](https://reliefweb.int/report/samoa/health-emergency-operation-centre-update-measles-outbreak-january-20-2020)
